items.content:
RT @snggle_: Was iPhone security broken just with Bluetooth?

iPhone was always known for its high security, second only to GrapheneOS. But a leaked Cellebrite document might show they found a way to break their protection.

The device is more vulnerable in AFU (After First Unlock) than in BFU (Before First Unlock). 
Cellebrite's "Advanced Unlock" allegedly has the capability to unlock devices in the AFU state. As a response to rising USB port protection, they answered with a method capable of bypassing encryption over the Bluetooth radio.

No pairing, no user interaction. The Bluetooth attack sends an L2CAP packet to the target that hijacks the Bluetooth daemon and gains kernel-level control.

What is interesting is that Apple patched this with the iPhone 17 and TOLD NO ONE. They implemented MIE (Memory Integrity Enforcement), which might also be proof that these alleged capabilities are real, and that devices older than the iPhone 17 are vulnerable to these attacks.

GrapheneOS documentation states that this attack vector is known and won't work on up-to-date GrapheneOS devices.

GrapheneOS will always be the safest option.

items.content:
RT @cr3ghost: Plex users: patch your servers.

Plex2Shell is a public unauthenticated RCE chain against Plex Media Server before 1.43.3.10861.

The chain combines 4 vulnerabilities:

- Unauthenticated SSRF
- Authentication / loopback pivot
- Transcoder SSRF + arbitrary-path file write
- Code execution through unsigned codec loading

The end result is unauthenticated remote code execution on the Plex server.

Especially important if your Plex instance is directly reachable from the internet. Normal Plex authentication should not be treated as protection against this chain.

Fixed in:
1.43.3.10861+

Research:
https://t.co/4qMLSACOLm

PoC / detections:
https://t.co/2Q4F5hPnCo

Credit: @zm_0x / Zach Main

items.content:
RT @nextronresearch: #APT28 is using weaponized Office documents to deliver the Covenant Grunt backdoor.

We detected a cluster of seven malicious .docm and .xls files between July 8 and July 14, with some having AV detection ratios as low as 5/62 at the time of first submission. Our THOR APT Scanner's YARA rules caught what traditional engines missed.

The documents use obfuscated VBA macros that assemble strings at runtime to evade static analysis, perform XOR-encoded host reconnaissance, and drop a 64-bit Covenant Grunt loader DLL disguised as a log file. The campaign uses Russian-language lures like "Прайс.xls" (Price List) and business-themed filenames like "accounts.xls", consistent with APT28 targeting patterns. Network analysis shows Dropbox being used as C2 infrastructure.

This activity aligns with Zscaler's reporting on Operation NeuSploit (CVE-2026-21509).

Analysis & IOCs: https://t.co/ALVVYK2ZZb

items.content:
BOUNDS is an interesting x86 asm instruction, not many know about.

Syntax:
  bounds <reg16 idx> ds:<ptr16/16 *min, *max>

Example:
 mov ax,15
 mov ds,segment
 mov si,array.header
 bounds ax,ds:[si]

Location contains the start/end of the array, and if we index outside of it, an exception is raised.

JB

items.content:
RT @MsftSecIntel: Microsoft Threat Intelligence is tracking an active supply chain attack in which a threat actor compromised the trusted OAuth App of the backup application ConnectWise Cloud Backup (AppId: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae), formerly SkyKick Backup, to obtain access tokens across customer tenants. 

ConnectWise Cloud Backup is a multitenant vendor application; customers grant consent for the application to operate in their tenants. We assess that the threat actor likely abused permissions previously granted by customers to the application, including highly elevated permissions like Directory.ReadWrite.All.

On October 15, 2026, we observed broad successful service principal authentication originating from the IP address 144.172.64[.]128. Follow-on activity included Microsoft Graph API reconnaissance and attempts to add additional credentials on the related service principal in target tenants to maintain direct access as a backdoor. 

Microsoft Defender detects post-exploitation activity with the following alerts:
- Any alert related to "Suspicious sign-in"
- Graph API activity from a Microsoft threat intelligence IP address 
- Verified Threat Actor IP

Defenders should review service principal sign-ins from unrecognized IP addresses, app credential changes, and OAuth grant activity associated with this specific OAuth AppId. In addition, we recommend looking for Threat Intelligence alerts on matching of IP against the Graph API activity and service principal activities. 

We will continue to monitor this incident and will share updates as they become available. We encourage customers to check ConnectWise advisory for more information and additional guidance: https://t.co/zwFyMAzaEV.

Indicators of compromise (IOCs): 
- App name: ConnectWise Cloud Backup  
- AppId: 506e08f9-6e9a-4da4-942b-a099a03644ae   
- Publisher name: SkyKick  
- Source IP: 144.172.64[.]128
- User agents: Python-urllib/3.12, python-requests/2.31, python-requests/2.34.2

items.content:
RT @m19o__: This is what happens when AI safety and alignment policies are designed without considering the people defending systems.

During the Hugging Face incident, commercial models blocked legitimate forensic analysis of real attack logs and payloads. They had to use a self-hosted GLM-5.2 to investigate the breach.

Now OpenCode is dealing with another security incident involving exposed AI provider keys, raising further questions about how dependent defenders are on the providers they rely on.

We’re past the point of using fearmongering about AI falling into the wrong hands to justify keeping advanced capabilities behind closed doors.

I’m not arguing against safeguards. I’m arguing that safeguards shouldn’t prevent legitimate security work.

If you don’t want to open-source your models, fine. At least establish a practical process that gives defenders access to the capabilities they need for research, testing, and incident response.

And by defenders, I mean everyone working in cybersecurity, not just a handful of organizations selected by AI labs.
